worksheet.title: Predict With Events
worksheet.subtitle: Guess both landings, then run to check
worksheet.learning_goal: I can predict where both sprites land by following the events that start them.

parts.title: Predict the whole chain
parts.text: Good coders predict before they run. The green flag starts Bit, and Bit's last block broadcasts 'go'. Pixel starts 'when I receive go'. To predict where BOTH land, follow the events: green flag → Bit moves and sends 'go' → Pixel hears 'go' and moves. Predict both, then run to check.

parts.title: Predict — before you run
parts.prompt: Follow the events in your head. PREDICT where each lands. Bit (home 1, forward 3) will land on: ____  Pixel (home 5, back 2) will land on: ____

parts.title: Run and check
parts.prompt: Now run it: click the flag, let Bit broadcast 'go', then run Pixel. Where did each really land? Bit: ____  Pixel: ____. Did your prediction match?

parts.title: What started Pixel?
parts.prompt: Pixel had no green-flag block. What event started Pixel's script? Write it.

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: Predicting with events means following the chain: which event starts the first script, what message it sends, and which script that message starts next. Then each sprite's moves tell you where it lands.

teacher_guide.eyebrow: Teacher Guide · Grade 2 · Events & Parallel Scripts
teacher_guide.title: Predict With Events
teacher_guide.subtitle: Quick facilitation notes & answer key

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: Students PREDICT the whole event chain before running: green flag starts Bit, Bit moves and sends a message, the message starts Pixel. A correct prediction names BOTH landings. No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start (no computer needed)
parts.text: No computer needed — paper and a pencil. You read the prompts aloud. Optional: two counters on a number line 0 to 5 (green Bit, purple Pixel), and a card that says "go" you can hand over to act out sending a message.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 20 minutes)
text: 1. Show them (you do). Follow the chain in your head: flag → Bit moves and sends "go" → Pixel runs.
2. Do one together. Exercise 1 — predict Bit on 4 and Pixel on 3.
3. Let them try. Students run to check (Ex 2), then name what started Pixel (Ex 3).

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
text: Exercise 2 (run) — the run confirms Bit on 4 and Pixel on 3.
Exercise 3 — Pixel was started by the message "go" (its "when I receive go" hat). The green flag only directly starts Bit; Pixel depends on Bit's message.

parts.title: If students get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: predicting only Bit. The chain ends with Pixel, so predict both.
Make it easier: predict Bit, follow the message, then predict Pixel.
Make it harder: ask them to predict whether the two meet.

parts.title: Ontario curriculum link (official wording)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential and concurrent events.
In plain terms: students write and run instructions that are started by an event, like clicking the green flag or getting a message.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential and concurrent events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.
In plain terms: students read instructions, change what starts them or one move, and explain what the change did.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The child predicts both landings by following the event chain, then checks by running.
